/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.headline: Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.excerpt: Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales. The imposition of new prison sanctions, coming into effect next year, builds on existing laws that order offenders to attend sentencing or face a fine or be jailed for a further two years for contempt of court. “Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences,” said the prisons minister, Catherine McKinnell. The new rules, to be laid before parliament on Thursday, will grant judges new powers to impose a loss of prison privileges for 84 days, cell confinement for 21 days, a loss of social visits for 27 days and a restriction on visits to once every four weeks, for 84 days. They could result in offenders already facing decades behind bars facing additional punishments. The Ministry of Justice has said that while no measure could guarantee offenders would attend their sentencing hearing, the widened powers strengthened the consequences for offenders and ensured they could be “appropriately punished”. Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, raised questions for ministers as to whether the new rules would achieve the aim of getting offenders to attend sentence hearings.
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.trail: England and Wales judges to be able to keep inmates in cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face victims’ families in court

/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.headline: Failure to fit tags left 5,000 offenders unmonitored in England and Wales, report finds
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.excerpt: More than 5,000 offenders went unmonitored in the first half of the year because electronic tags were not installed, while 1,600 tags had no signal for more than two weeks due to faults, a report has found. The Institute for Government (IfG) has revealed the full scale of the crisis in the probation system in England and Wales, concluding that “rationing probation supervision” due to a lack of staff meant sentences imposed by the court had become “essentially a fiction” for most offenders. Once the 2026 Sentencing Act – which reduces the release point for many sentences – is fully implemented, most offenders will spend the final third of their sentence on licence without any active supervision, the report said. “This risks further undermining public trust in the criminal justice system and making sentences even more convoluted and opaque, including to victims,” the report by the independent thinktank found. Cassia Rowland, the associate director at the institute and author of the report, said: “It’s hard to set out just how demoralised and unhappy a lot of probation staff are. They feel everything is really chaotic, all of these changes are being flung on to them, they’re worried about their personal safety and the public protection risk of the people they’re managing.” She added: “The sentences courts are imposing are having less and less relevance to the time people are actually serving.
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.trail: In first half of this year 1,600 tags also had no signal for over two weeks, highlighting scale of probation crisis

/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.headline: Two men serving indefinite jail sentences freed after two decades
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.excerpt: Two men jailed with indefinite sentences for public protection (IPPs) have been freed after each serving about two decades in custody despite receiving minimum terms of two years or less. A high court judge and a magistrate hearing an appeal after a review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) told Luke Ings and Liam Bennett they would be freed, and also replaced an indeterminate sentence given to a third man, James Ward. Ward, who was freed in 2017 after serving 10 years more than his one-year minimum and was later recalled to prison, was also in court, sitting in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced. Relatives of Ings and Bennett hugged in the public gallery at Wolverhampton crown court on Wednesday as Mr Justice Choudhury told them the IPPs had been “cancelled”. Choudhury said Bennett would instead be sentenced to four years and 264 days, Ward to two years, and Ings to 42 months with a 30-month extended licence. All three men’s original sentences were quashed and replaced after they argued that judges had wrongly found them to be dangerous or had not considered alternative sentences. Choudhury, sitting with the magistrate Norma Grant, told the appellants: “You have already spent considerably longer than those [replacement] sentences in custody.
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.trail: Convicted pair, plus third man released in August, have IPPs replaced after serving much longer than minimum terms

/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.headline: More sex offenders in England and Wales could be released amid court system crisis, police sources say
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.excerpt: More sexual predators in England and Wales could be freed instead of jailed because of the pressure on courts and prisons, police sources have told the Guardian. The warning comes after the Metropolitan police commissioner, Mark Rowley, on Thursday condemned the release on bail of a man after he admitted taking pictures of children and women, and then using AI to sexualise them. Zafer Dogan was bailed to his flat overlooking a children’s playground, from which he committed some of the offences he admitted, despite prosecutors and police saying he should be remanded in custody. One of his victims said they had to move after courts declined to send him to jail ahead of his sentencing on Thursday, where he was imprisoned for two years. A senior police source said they feared more such cases across England and Wales, where charged suspects are released rather than jailed: “We are bracing ourselves for more of this across the country, that is, offenders who should be remanded, instead being freed on bail, to the distress of their victims. “Some forces are better resourced to deal with this than others. It is going to be a nationwide issue.” The government’s early release policy, to ease pressure on prisons where places are on the verge of running out, is expected to start next Thursday. The police source added: “Probation is crumbling, policing is having to pick up extra offender management work which it has not had to do before. Something has got to give.
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.trail: Sources tell the Guardian they are braced for more offenders being bailed into the community ahead of October’s early prisoner release

/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.headline: What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.excerpt: Grooming gang perpetrators and killers, including those responsible for PC Andrew Harper’s death, will be blocked from early prison release under changes announced by Andy Burnham after a backlash over the scope of the scheme. Here is a primer on how the crisis unfolded and what the upshot of Burnham’s decision could be. What is happening to prison sentences? From 1 October 2026, a change to sentencing rules means some adults serving a standard prison sentence in England and Wales will be released earlier than the date originally planned, the Institute for Government explains. “Prisoners convicted of less serious offences, who currently spend 40% or 50% of their sentence in prison, will leave prison after a third of their sentence. A second group, currently released after two-thirds of their sentence, will leave after half,” the IfG says. “Leaving prison does not end the sentence. The person serves the rest of their sentence in the community on licence, under conditions set by probation, and can be returned to prison if those conditions are breached.” Murderers or people handed life or extended sentences have never been included in any proposals for reducing sentences and will stay locked up until they go before the Parole Board. Why is this happening? The Labour government says it inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse, with fewer than 100 spaces left in the summer of 2024.
/law/2026/nov/05/henry-nowak-killer-vick.trail: Offences including manslaughter have been excluded from changes to sentencing rules amid an overcrowding crisis

/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.headline: ‘I’m always being real’: what on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.excerpt: In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency”. Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors. “The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives”. It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0”, which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says. That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew? Some people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace.
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.trail: With You Can See Everything, Holmes joins other such high-profile subjects as Lance Armstrong, Imelda Marcos and Anthony Weiner to allow film-makers to document their lives. But do they ever come out well?

/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.headline: 55,000 fans and nowhere to hide: what it’s like to play in basketball’s biggest arena
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.excerpt: Jamie Malonzo got there early, one of the first players to arrive. He knew this was a different thing altogether. He knew the 55,000-capacity Philippine Arena was something else. As Malonzo warmed up, the crowd began to file into the stands for Game 7 of the PBA Commissioner’s Cup. Fans tried to get his attention, yelling and waving their arms madly. This game, Malonzo knew, would be unlike any other he had ever played in. “For me, warming up in there was not about trying to warm up my body. It was more about practicing cancelling out the outside noise – it was like practicing a different part of your brain,” the Seattle-born forward says of the game in January 2023. When the game started, things didn’t get any easier. “It was definitely hard to hear,” the 30-year-old says. “I remember that being a problem.” In fact, Malonzo and his team had to invent hand signals to combat the fan volume. “When you were on the court and you look up and you see these people way, way, way, way, up there in the upper bleachers cheering – it was crazy,” he says. Today, most professional basketball arenas seat between 10,000 and 20,000 people. The capacity at Madison Square Garden, for example, is 19,812 for New York Knicks games. The Philippine Arena seats nearly three times that. Until this month, it was the largest indoor arena in the world.
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.trail: The sprawling Philippine Arena hosts games in a country of fanatical basketball fans. Jamie Malonzo was lucky enough to play there in a Game 7

/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.headline: Forgotten Island review – best friends forever trapped in frantic DreamWorks animation
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.excerpt: Frantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm. The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline. Their alliance is pledged and a friendship bracelet woven, but as the years go by, poor Jo winds up with a loser’s job in a fast food joint, whereas Raissa feels guilty about leaving Jo behind as she heads for college at Caltech in the glamorous world of America.
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.trail: This over-controlled adventure never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life

/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.headline: Philippine school shooter kills fellow student and himself in livestreamed attack
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.excerpt: A student livestreamed himself shooting and killing another pupil in a classroom in the southern Philippines before taking his own ⁠life, the second school attack in the country in less than two months. The shooting took ⁠place at a school attached to Ateneo de Zamboanga University in the southern city of ⁠Zamboanga, a Catholic private institution in western Mindanao. Zamboanga city’s mayor, Khymer Adan Olaso, told the DZMM radio station that the ‌shooter “managed to enter carrying a high-powered firearm and a .45-calibre pistol”. The interior secretary, Victor Remulla, confirmed the ninth-grade suspect had livestreamed the attack on social media. The shooter’s Facebook account has since been disabled. In the video, which was circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun is seen moving down a hallway before it is pointed into a classroom and fired. Children in school uniforms are seen screaming and rushing for an exit. National police are now trying to “establish the motive behind the shooting, determine the ownership and source of the firearm used, and find out how it was brought inside the school campus”, the interior ministry said. Hours later, the Philippines’ customs department said it had ordered the “preventive suspension” of an agent who owned the guns “allegedly used by the student involved”. The customs deputy chief of staff, Noel Bendijo, told AFP that customs staff had acted on intelligence from their own officers in Zamboanga.
/world/2026/nov/05/meghan-sussex-thomas-.trail: Country’s second fatal school shooting in two months took place in southern city of ⁠Zamboanga

/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.headline: Ryanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costs
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.excerpt: Ryanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict. The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive. Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028. “Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.” Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $106 a barrel on Monday. Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire. “To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.trail: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures

/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.headline: Almost a quarter of European airline pilots fly when too fatigued to work
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.excerpt: Three in four European airline pilots have taken microsleeps in the cockpit, while almost a quarter routinely fly despite being too fatigued to work, according to a report. The findings, based on a survey of almost 7,200 captains and first officers by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), include pilots reporting insufficient rest, pressure to extend working hours and fears of being penalised for declaring themselves unfit to fly. Almost a quarter (24%) of pilots admitted they usually continue flying rather than report themselves unfit due to fatigue, while another 16.8% said they call in sick instead. In aviation, fatigue can result from long duty hours, insufficient rest, irregular schedules and flying across time zones, which disrupt the body’s natural sleep cycle. It is a significant safety concern because it can impair pilots’ judgment, slow their reactions, reduce alertness and impair responses to unexpected situations. Under European aviation safety regulations, airlines are required to have systems in place to identify, monitor and manage crew fatigue. The survey, conducted in August, found that three-quarters of respondents had experienced at least one microsleep – a brief, involuntary episode of sleep – while operating an aircraft in the previous four weeks. Pilots working for airlines based in Ireland and Malta reported the highest levels of microsleeps. More than a third said they were not getting enough rest to prevent fatigue from building up over time.
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.trail: Pilots report pressure to extend working hours and fears of penalties for declaring themselves unfit to fly

/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.headline: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.excerpt: Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict. Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%. “You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels. Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be 70% higher across 2026 – estimated to average $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits. Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February. However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high.
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.trail: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says

/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.headline: Fewer Britons plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, says travel industry
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.excerpt: The UK’s cost of living squeeze means fewer people plan to ringfence money for holidays abroad next year, the travel industry has warned. Despite war, wildfires and EES border checks, the numbers of Britons taking holidays climbed back to pre-pandemic levels this year – but rising costs may mean the numbers have peaked, according to an annual travel industry report on Tuesday. Numbers taking holidays at home and abroad continued to rise, although late bookings and shorter city breaks have been an increasing feature of holidays through 2026. Confidence in travel dropped slightly year on year but rebounded as fears over jet fuel shortages and flight disruption faded since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran in February, according to research from the industry body Abta. Overall, 88% of Brits took a holiday this year, matching the 2019 pre-pandemic peak, with a new high of 74% in the UK and 62% abroad. However, Abta’s report found that almost one in three people were planning to spend less on travelling abroad next year, suggesting that the annual holiday is no longer sacrosanct. Fewer people now say they are willing to reduce spending on phones or other gadgets than the holiday abroad. Abta said the holiday business remained resilient, despite a dip in its travel confidence index to +50 – this measures the net proportion of people who felt secure in going abroad, compared with those who were worried.
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.trail: Spain remains most popular destination as Britons book later in hope of better deals, Abta report finds

/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.headline: Flight chaos for hundreds of thousands was caused in ‘millisecond’ by software error
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.excerpt: A software defect in part of the UK’s air traffic control system corrupted flight data “in the space of a millisecond”, leading to a six-hour outage and mass airline cancellations and delays across the UK last week, National Air Traffic Services has said. But ministers said the Nats report into the incident still left questions unanswered, saying they needed “to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos”. According to the report, the error first occurred at 10am and was notified to engineers who investigated – but the system appeared to be working again, until 12.30pm when a repeat occurred and a major incident was declared. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) industry regulator would now “check their findings” and investigate Nats more widely. Hundreds of thousands of passengers had their travel disrupted after the Nats failure on Tuesday 8 September, which ended up delaying and cancelling flights across the UK and beyond late into the next day. Airlines have called for compensation and a “credible plan”, with Ryanair demanding the dismissal of the Nats chief executive officer, Martin Rolfe, after the third major air traffic control failure in the UK since summer 2023. A government source said the CAA review would be “a chance to fundamentally investigate” if Nats was fit for purpose. Rolfe said the incident was unrelated to the previous failures.
/world/2026/nov/05/bomb-threats-disrupt-.trail: Error first occurred at 10am but major incident was not declared until 12.30pm, says report

/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.headline: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.excerpt: The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials. As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies. “We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment. “It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said. Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said.
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.trail: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment

/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.headline: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.excerpt: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country. The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added. The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history. The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public. The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.trail: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.headline: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as virus ‘surges’ in DR Congo province
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.excerpt: Kenya has reported its first-ever Ebola death, the health minister announced on Tuesday, as the disease continues to spread rapidly through the north-east of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where the outbreak was announced in May. This is the 17th outbreak of the highly infectious, often deadly disease in the DRC. As of 2 October, 4,082 people had died out of 8,463 confirmed cases in the country since the emergence of the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, for which there is still no vaccine nor specific treatment. A Kenyan man who had been living in the DRC for seven years died after returning to Kenya, the Kenyan health minister Aden Duale told reporters. The man, who has not been named, had been treated in the DRC after falling ill about a month ago. He then travelled overland to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, before flying to Nairobi on 3 October. Kenya has previously never reported a case of Ebola, but neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 – almost all people who had travelled from the DRC – and two deaths, before being declared Ebola-free in August. Duale said the man was taken by a relative and a friend from Nairobi’s international airport to Nairobi hospital, where he was immediately isolated, suffering from “fever, chills, intense fatigue, weakness, muscle pain, painful swallowing, sore throat and bleeding under the skin at the injection sites”.
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.trail: Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday

/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.headline: DRC politician beaten to death after radio appearance about Ebola outbreak
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.excerpt: A senior member of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s ruling party was beaten to death on Sunday after appearing on a radio programme to raise awareness about the Ebola outbreak, a party representative has said. Marie-Celestin Karondwa, the acting president of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) party’s federal executive committee in Butembo, a new hotspot for the outbreak, was attacked after taking part in a radio show during which he ‌promoted prevention measures for the disease, ‌the UDPS federation in the city said in a statement, Reuters reported. The party ‌said the attackers beat Karondwa, stole his belongings and set his house on fire, and that he later died from his injuries. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many people were involved or what motivated it, but the party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended ‌the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”. Karondwa’s death comes after a series of attacks on healthcare workers and treatment centres that experts say are fuelled by rumours and misinformation about the disease and distrust of health responders. The incidents have included violence, riots and property damage and the disruption of essential services.
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.trail: Marie-Celestin Karondwa was attacked on Sunday after promoting measures to prevent spread of disease, his party says

/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.headline: Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow
/world/2026/nov/05/british-ebola-patient.excerpt: Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak. For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials. Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola. “We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day. “It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said. Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease. The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease.

/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.headline: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.excerpt: People from minority ethnic backgrounds in England are up to a third less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via routine screening, and are more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting, analysis has found. The research, carried out by academics at the University of Surrey and funded by the charity Breast Cancer Now, involved analysis of 86,564 adults diagnosed with the disease between 2009 and 2019, from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink and the Cancer Registration Tumour and Treatment datasets. The analysis found that people from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds, alongside people from deprived backgrounds, were up to 33% less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, while these groups were also up to 31% more likely to be diagnosed via urgent suspected cancer referral, and up to 37% more likely to be diagnosed via emergency presentation. Manveet Basra, the associate director of public health, inclusion and awareness at Breast Cancer Now, said the analysis revealed that people from marginalised groups “face inequalities at every stage of their breast cancer experience, and tragically this impacts their survival rates”. Basra added: “This research helps us understand who is less likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer via screening, [who] might wait longer to get diagnosed or experience delays in treatment, and knowing what barriers they face enables us to work towards eliminating them.
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.trail: Exclusive: People from marginalised groups more likely to be diagnosed via urgent referral or in emergency setting, research finds

/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.headline: Woman told she had cancer by NHS worker who inappropriately accessed her records
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.excerpt: A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee she barely knew who had accessed her medical records days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant. Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall hospital in Truro. Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said her personal information was accessed by a man she knew only vaguely who worked at the hospital. She said: “I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. This man said to me: ‘Pippa, I don’t want you to worry, but you’ve got cancer.’ I just couldn’t really believe it.” Two days later, Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer. Boardman, who is recovering well from the cancer, said Royal Cornwall’s handling of the case had reinforced her trauma, and she said the trust only apologised once it had been contacted by reporters at the BBC. She told the BBC: “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.” A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.trail: Pippa Boardman said she lost her dignity through data breach at Royal Cornwall hospital by man she barely knew

/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.headline: UK doctors develop non-invasive test for womb cancer in women bleeding after menopause
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.excerpt: Doctors have developed a simple test that could help rule out womb cancer in women who experience bleeding after menopause. The approach has the potential to transform care for thousands of women each year and spare them from invasive and uncomfortable tests that can also be costly for healthcare systems. Every year, hundreds of thousands of women worldwide are diagnosed with womb cancer. Bleeding after menopause triggers an urgent cancer referral but only about 5% to 10% of women who report bleeding have an underlying cancer. Currently, the tests for womb cancer – an internal ultrasound scan, a biopsy of the womb lining and hysteroscopy, in which a camera is passed into the womb – are all invasive and costly. The new test, developed at the University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS foundation trust, looks at cells collected from the urine and vaginal fluid. It is cheap and non-invasive. In a study assessing the test, 1,864 women attending seven hospitals in north-west England with postmenopausal bleeding gave a urine sample and a vaginal fluid sample before their routine tests. Of these women, 5% (99 of the 1,864) were diagnosed with womb cancer via a biopsy or surgery. Using the new test, cytologists unaware of the women’s diagnoses identified 80 of the 99 womb cancers and correctly returned a negative result for 93% of women who did not have womb cancer. The findings were published in the journal Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women’s Health.
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.trail: Test using urine and vaginal fluid samples raises hopes thousands of lower-risk women could be spared internal ultrasounds and hysteroscopies

/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.headline: ‘Early deaths are not inevitable’: report reveals why adults with severe mental illness die younger
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.excerpt: An analysis of NHS data has shed light on the “scandal” of why adults with severe mental illness are more likely to die 15 to 20 years younger than the general population. The Rethink Mental Illness charity has revealed that adults under 75 with serious mental ill health – defined as those referred to specialist secondary mental health services – are 6.3 times as likely to die from liver disease, 6 times more likely from respiratory illness, 3.8 times more likely from cardiovascular disease and 2.3 times as likely from cancer. They are also 14.6 times as likely to die due to suicide, compared with those who were not referred. Overall, they are 4.8 times more likely to die of any cause before the age of 75 than the general population. For some conditions, these health inequalities are the starkest to date. For working-age adults living with a mental illness, the number of deaths from cardiovascular disease and cancer are at their highest levels since records began, each with more than 24,000 deaths in the 2022-2024 reporting period, the charity calculated. Cancer, cardiovascular disease, liver disease and respiratory disease accounted for more than half (56.5%) of deaths for 18- to 74-year-olds with severe mental health problems in England during this period. Cancer and cardiovascular disease each accounted for just under 19% of all deaths, respiratory disease 11%, and liver disease 8%. During the same period, suicide comprised 7% of these early deaths.
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.trail: Exclusive: Charity says NHS data shows increased chances of death due to preventable physical illnesses

/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.headline: Women in England with incurable breast cancer to get life-extending drug on NHS
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.excerpt: Thousands of women in England with incurable breast cancer will get access to a life-extending drug on the NHS after negotiations over its cost proved successful. About 1,000 women a year with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will be able to obtain Enhertu from Thursday after ministers and the drug’s makers struck a deal on its price. About one in seven of the 60,000 new cases of breast cancer diagnosed every year in the UK are HER2-positive. Clinical trials have shown that Enhertu almost doubled median progression-free survival compared with normal chemotherapy, from 5.1 months to 9.9 months. Median overall survival among people who used it was 23.4 months, compared with 16.8 months among those not on it – a 6.6-month gain. “This is a momentous day for thousands of people who will now have access to a drug that will give them the opportunity to gain precious time with loved ones”, said Claire Rowney, the chief executive of Breast Cancer Now. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) announced on Thursday that about 1,000 patients a year in England will be eligible to receive the treatment from the NHS after it recommended it for routine use. Nice, which advises the NHS on whether treatments represent value for money, had previously rejected Enhertu, in July 2024, as too expensive to justify, despite its proven effectiveness.
/society/2026/nov/05/nhs-england-cancer-.trail: Thousands with HER2-low advanced breast cancer will have access to Enhertu after ministers strike deal on price

/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.headline: Deep-red Kansas votes for change as patience wears thin with Trump: ‘The economy is really taking a beating’
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.excerpt: Linda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry. In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump. She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House. But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year. “I thought at the time that he was the better choice of what we had,” Olson said of Trump in 2024. Instead, he had been acting to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”. With frustrations like these looming large across the state, Kansans this week elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It was a stunning upset in what was, until recently, thought to be a reliably red stronghold. “I’ve seen what Roger Marshall did over the eight years or so that he’s been doing this,” said Olson, of the defeated Republican senator.
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.trail: Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run

/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.headline: Trump tries to get 2024 conviction in hush-money corruption case thrown out
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.excerpt: Donald Trump’s legal team on Thursday continued efforts to get his 2024 conviction in the hush-money election corruption case thrown out. Attorneys for the US president are trying to persuade a New York appeals court to toss the criminal trial verdict from May 2024, when Trump was found guilty on all charges of falsifying business records in the hush-money corruption scheme to influence his eventual victory in the 2016 presidential election. The felony conviction came after the jury agreed he altered records in order to obscure a $130,000 payment to buy the silence of adult film performer and producer Stormy Daniels. Trump mentioned the case again on social media as recently as September. He was already the president-elect for his second term in office in early January 2025 when the judge in the case gave Trump an unconditional discharge, meaning he would remain a convicted felon but was given no jail time, fine or other penalty. The president has always denied any wrongdoing and has turned to state and federal courts in hopes of unwinding the verdict. He was not expected to attend Thursday’s court session. The trial involved the fee that Daniels received from Trump’s then fixer and lawyer, Michael Cohen, weeks before the 2016 election. The money bought, for a time, her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier when he was already married to Melania Trump and she had given birth to his youngest son, Barron.
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.trail: President’s lawyers ask appeals court to toss criminal trial verdict over $130,000 sent to Stormy Daniels

/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.headline: Republicans hoping to succeed Trump in 2028 dissect midterm rout
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.excerpt: Republican hopefuls in the race to succeed Donald Trump swiftly blamed two key pillars of his agenda – the Iran war and tariffs – for summoning the Democratic blue wave that swept the US midterm elections. The fallout from the stunning success of Democrats on Tuesday night has left Republicans reeling – and grasping for the reasons behind the collapse in support. On Thursday, the Associated Press called more competitive House races for the Democrats, though Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remained undecided. Vice-president JD Vance, the outgoing Florida governor Ron DeSantis, and Texas senator Ted Cruz all pointed to frustration over cost of living amid the fallout from Republican defeats across the country, including in previous strongholds such as Texas and Kansas. They cited factors including Trump’s prolonged war on Iran and aggressive trade agenda; the US-Israel relationship; and Democratic ads that painted conservative candidates poorly. “Tariffs have made everything too expensive and the Iran war has dragged on too long,” Cruz, a former Republican presidential candidate who has not ruled out another run, said on his podcast, Verdict With Ted Cruz, on Wednesday. “It should have been brief, decisive and over. It needs to end.” “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote in a lengthy X post on Wednesday, suggesting his party lost because voters are angry at the Trump administration for diverting focus away from Americans.
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.trail: JD Vance, Ron DeSantis and Ted Cruz all pointed to Iran war and affordability as key factors in Democratic victory

/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.headline: Europe’s far right has a Trump problem after Republican US midterms wipeout
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.excerpt: The historic Republican defeat in the US midterm elections has forcibly reminded Europe’s far-right leaders of their perennial Donald Trump dilemma: they may love his nativist agenda, but the man himself is a toxic electoral liability. Since his re-election in 2024, European populist leaders such as Marine Le Pen in France and Giorgia Meloni in Italy have carefully calibrated their public postures towards the US president, walking a delicate transatlantic tightrope. They adore his policies on hard borders, culture wars and anti-globalism. But European voters, even on the far right, detest Trump’s personal volatility, geopolitical unpredictability, unreliability on Europe’s defence, and trade protectionism. Trump’s territorial threats over Greenland and economic nationalism have proved particular problems: no leader who champions national sovereignty and domestic jobs could back threats to invade the largely self-governing territory of an EU member state or punitive trade tariffs. The sheer scale of Tuesday’s Republican wipeout has now prompted Europe’s populists to distance themselves yet further while taking away one big lesson: angry, economically squeezed voters topple incumbents. Across European capitals on Wednesday, far-right politicians were actively insulating themselves from the White House, while dutifully avoiding any personal attacks.
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.trail: European far-right leaders quick to distance themselves from US president and stress their own priorities

/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.headline: Trump-backed Republicans lose dozens of US midterm races, raising questions over his influence
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.excerpt: Dozens of Republican candidates directly endorsed by Donald Trump lost their US midterm election races, according to analysis by the Guardian, raising questions over the power of the president’s support. In past elections, Trump’s endorsements have been coveted. In the final stages of this year’s campaign, he actively urged voters to act as though he were on the ballot. But just half of the 26 candidates Trump endorsed for the US Senate had won their elections as of Wednesday at 5pm ET, according to a Guardian tally. Of the 23 candidates for state governor endorsed by Trump, only nine had won their elections. Twelve were defeated, with two races still to be called. The president’s endorsed House candidates fared better, with roughly 60% winning their races, although many in competitive House districts were defeated. In total, 46 Trump-backed candidates for the House have lost so far, with Trump’s tumbling approval ratings appearing to challenge the influence of his public support for Republican candidates. Over the last decade, Trump has reshaped the Republican party in the mold of his Make America Great Again (Maga) vision, handpicking loyal candidates to run in competitive races and occasionally rejecting established Republicans. The US president’s base has been loyal to his choices. In 2022, approximately 82% of candidates endorsed by Trump went on to win their race, according to the New York Times.
/us-news/2026/nov/05/trump-oval-office-d.trail: Guardian analysis shows how tumbling approval ratings may have hurt candidates backed by US president
